---
title: Real Options
output: pdf_document
---

Using just NPV analysis for project valuation does not take into account the
fact that real projects are dynamic and changes in circumstances can affect
value. For instance, a project can be expanded if it proves to be successful or
abandoned if not. NPV analysis does not take this into account and usually
undervalues projects. In this section we will explore real options,
specifically the option to expand, the option to abandon, and the timing
option.

# The option to expand

The book uses the example of opening an ice hotel to explain the option to
expand. The initial investment was found to be \$12 million and the cash flow
in perpetuity will be \$2 million. The discount rate to use is 20 percent.
Based on these figures we can calculate the NPV

$$
-\$12,000,000 + \$2,000,000 / .20 = -\$2 \text{ million}
$$

Based on strict NPV, we would reject this project. Now the \$2 million annual
cash flow is based on the expected value from two forecasts:

* __Optimistic forecast:__ $-\$12 \text{ million} + \$3 \text{ million} / .20 =
  \$3 \text{ million}$

* __Pessimistic forecast:__ $-\$12 \text{ million} + \$1 \text{ million} / .20
  = -\$7 \text{ million}$

We calculate the expected value:

$$
50\% \times \$3 \text{ million} + 50\% \times (-\$7 \text{ million})
  = -\$2 \text{ million}
$$

But what if the optimistic forecast turns out to be correct. We may want an
option to expand the ice hotel operation into say 10 locations. A simplified
calculation can be made (assuming the unlikely situation where we build all 10
hotels at once):

$$
50\% \times 10 \times \$3 \text{ million} + 50\% \times (-\$7 \text{ million})
  = \$11.5 \text{ million}
$$

The value of the option is the difference between the two calculations:

$$
\$11.5 \text{ million} - (-\$2 \text{ million}) = \$13.5 \text{ million}
$$

Now the expected NPV looks a lot better, and thus the project should go
forward.

# The option to abandon

On the other hand, what if there is a 50 percent chance the annual cash flows
will be \$6 million and a 50 percent chance the annual cash flows will be -\$2
million. We calculate the two forecasts as:

* __Optimistic forecast:__ $-\$12 \text{ million} + \$6 \text{ million} / .2 =
  \$18 \text{ million}$
* __Pessimistic forecast:__ $-\$12 \text{ million} - \$2 \text{ million} / .2 =
  -\$22 \text{ million}$

The expected NPV for the project:

$$
50\% \times \$18 \text{ million} + 50\% \times (-\$22 \text{ million})
  = -\$2 \text{ million}
$$

Again, because the NPV is negative we should not go ahead with the project. But
what if we consider the option to abandon the project if, after one year, we
find out that the pessimistic forecast comes true. Then we can recalculate the
NPV, using the present value of just one year for the pessimistic forecast:

$$
50\% \times \$18 \text{ million} + 50\% \times (-\$12 \text{ million}
  - \$2 \text{ million} / 1.20) = \$2.17 \text{ million}
$$

Again the value of the option is the difference between these two NPV calculations

$$
\$2.17 \text{ million} - (-\$2 \text{ million}) = \$4.17 \text{ million}
$$

With the option to abandon, we do not have to experience the negative cash flow
for the later years if the pessimistic forecast turns true for the first year.
The NPV turns positive and we should proceed with the project.

# Timing options

The book uses a different example for this option type. That of an empty plot
of land. What if we bought a plot of land and the best use of the land would be
to build an office building and charge rent. If construction costs were
estimated to be \$1 million and total net rent (after all costs) were estimated
to be \$90,000 per year in perpetuity. We will use a discount rate of 10
percent. We can calculate the NPV to be:

$$
-\$1 \text{ million} + \$90,000 / .10 = -\$100,000
$$

The negative NPV indicates that we should not build. But what if the federal
government is planning on implementing an urban revitalization program for the
city. If this program succeeds then we could charge higher rent. If the program
does not succeed we will not build. This is called a _timing option_. Although
we do not want to currently build, we want the option to build in the future if
the environment proves to be favorable. The timing option is why vacant land
has value. Even though there are costs such as maintenance of the land, taxes,
etc. Holding onto the land with a timing option to build can substantially
raise the value of the property. The book doesn't value this option. It only
explains why waiting can be worth more than building today.

Another example of timing options is in mining. Suppose you own a copper mine,
but the price of copper does not justify the cost of mining at the moment. You
would still want to hold onto the mine and wait for a more favorable price.

# Conclusion

Real options allow you to take dynamic and changing circumstances into account
when valuing a project. Static NPV tends to undervalue projects. In the real
world, restaurant owners have the option to close if the restaurant does not
prove fruitful. On the other hand if the restaurant is a success, an owner may
want to open more restaurants in other locations. Maybe franchise the
operations and license to others.

This section demonstrates how to value some simple option examples. The values
and probabilities were given and the calculations are easy to perform. In the
real world probabilities and outcomes are not known. Most of the time you have
to make educated guesses based on the information you have. Also, knowing when
you have arrived at an outcome may be uncertain. A year may not be enough time
to know if your restaurant will succeed or not. Finally, the discount rate is
uncertain as well. The option to expand or abandon the project changes the
project's risk, and therefore the discount rate. Option values are only as
reliable as these assumptions.

We can see similarities between real options and financial options. For
instance the option to expand is similar to buying a call option to buy
shares of stock if the price exceeds the strike price. The option to abandon is
like buying a put option to sell shares of stock if the price falls below the
strike price. The timing option is also like a call option. If the price proves
favorable at a future date, you may want to buy the stock.

Real options are usually represented as a decision tree which will be discussed
in the next section.
